children: , the integrated energy producer, jumped approximately 2.1% to $216.58 Tuesday afternoon as Brent crude climbed to $109.20 per barrel. The move came as Saudi export disruptions, Libyan outages and fresh attacks on energy infrastructure tightened the market's focus on supply risk. The valuation picture is already stretched, however: Chevron's $216.58 share price sits 33.55% above its GuruFocus GF Value of $162.17, suggesting investors are paying a sizable premium for the current energy backdrop.

Chevron's second-quarter results delivered $12.1 billion of earnings while worldwide production climbed 20%. The company also cut debt by $8.4 billion, reached record U.S. production and signed a 20-year power agreement with Microsoft tied to a West Texas data-center project. That combination gives Chevron two powerful earnings levers: traditional oil-and-gas cash flow today and potential exposure to the AI infrastructure buildout over a much longer runway.

That distinction matters. Higher crude prices can boost Chevron's cash generation quickly, helping fund dividends, buybacks and future projects, while the Microsoft agreement opens a completely different path into surging data-center electricity demand. But the market is already pricing in plenty of optimism. With the shares trading more than one-third above GF Value, investors are effectively betting that strong commodity economics and new power opportunities can justify a valuation well above GuruFocus' estimate of intrinsic value.

title: Chevron Jumps 2.1% as $109 Oil Funds Its AI-Power Pivot
